paper_title: Do learned image captioning metrics generalize? Auditing duplicated samples in human-judgment benchmarks

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Learned image captioning metrics are trained and tested on human judgments, so their reported correlation is a claim about generalization. We audit this claim for the three most recent collections of such judgments, Polaris, Nebula, and Spica, matching images at the pixel level. First, test samples reappear in training sets: the Spica training set contains about two-thirds of the Polaris test set, with identical human ratings. Second, controlled retraining shows that duplicates can inflate a metric: for Pearl, the gain is confined to the duplicated samples and grows with every epoch; for DENEB, it stays below one point. The gain depends on the learner and on how often a training set repeats a sample. Third, Kendall's $τ$ over all samples is the sum of two terms, detecting captions with the lowest human score and ranking the others; the first supplies most of the reported correlation and is nearly saturated. The recent test sets cannot order Polos, DENEB and Pearl consistently, and a ridge regression on frozen features matches or exceeds all three. Fourth, we propose a protocol that ranks a learned metric only with a model trained without test samples, reports both terms, and compares metrics by paired tests. Under it, zero-shot vision--language judges rank first on the three recent test sets, and a fine-tuned judge ranks first on the three earlier benchmarks. The same analysis applies to any evaluator learned from human judgments; filter lists and code are released at https://github.com/morninghut/ic-dataset-audit .

Introduction Automatic metrics decide which image captioning model is reported as better [1 3]. Increasingly, the metrics are themselves learned: Polos [4], DENEB [5] and Pearl [6] regress human scores from the features of pretrained encoders, and Rigel [7] fine-tunes visionlanguage model (VLM) for the same purpose. learned metric is pattern recognition model like any other. Its correlation with human scores on test set is therefore statement about generalization, and it deserves the scrutiny that the field applies to classifiers: is the test set independent of the training set, and what does the reported number measure? This line of work became possible through three collections of human judgments, Polaris, Nebula and Spica, released with Polos, DENEB and Pearl. Together, they provide several hundred thousand ratings, far more than any earlier benchmark, and they are the reason learned metrics can be trained at all. The collections were built in sequence and draw on shared source images, and later papers also report earlier metrics on the newer test sets: Polos, for example, is baseline on the Nebula test set in the papers of DENEB, Pearl and Rigel. If samples of test set are also present in the training set of another collection, metric evaluated across collections is partly tested on what it was trained on. To help the community use these resources reliably across generations, we examine whether this happens and what follows from it. Fig. 1 summarizes the study in three steps, each of which answers one question. Are test samples in the training sets? Yes, across collections. About two-thirds of the Polaris test set is contained in the Spica training set and half of it in the Nebula training set; in the other direction, the Polaris training set contains large parts of the Spica and Nebula test sets. The duplicated samples carry the same human ratings on both sides. Within collection and on the earlier benchmarks, Flickr8k and Composite, we find almost none. Does this change the measured correlation? It can, and how much depends on the metric. For Pearl, the gain from the duplicates sits on the duplicated samples and 2 Figure 1: Overview of the study. Learned metrics are ranked only with deduplicated model, Kendalls 𝜏 is reported over all samples and over samples above the lowest human score, and metrics are compared by paired tests before 33 metrics are re-ranked. grows with every training epoch, while the other samples of the same test set stay flat. For DENEB, the gain is below one point, and for the released Rigel checkpoint we detect none. Cross-fitting three further learners shows the pattern behind this: the more model can memorize, and the more often the training set repeats sample, the more duplicate is worth. What do the benchmarks measure once duplicates are set aside? quarter or more of every evaluation set consists of captions with the lowest human score, most of them obvious mismatches. Kendalls 𝜏 over all samples decomposes exactly into term for detecting these samples and term for ranking the others. Detection is necessary ability, but modern metrics have nearly saturated it, and it supplies most of the reported number. On the ranking term, the recent test sets do not separate Polos, DENEB and Pearl. ridge regression on frozen features, the simplest model that can be fitted to human scores, matches or exceeds all three on each of these test sets. Under protocol that removes duplicates and reports both terms, zero-shot VLMs used as judges rank first on the recent test sets, and fine-tuned judge on the earlier benchmarks. Scope. The audit concerns one family of collections, but the question is general: evaluators learned from human judgments are now common in machine translation, summarization, and image quality assessment, and their benchmarks also grow by extending earlier ones. We intend this study as worked example of how the generalization of such an evaluator can be measured with statistical care, and as contribution to the discussion in pattern recognition on what benchmark number means [8, 9]. We do not claim that published results are wrong. Each of the four papers evaluates its metric on sets that its own training set does not duplicate, and we reproduce their numbers (Appendix A). What duplication affects is the comparison across collections. Our contributions are: content-level audit of three training sets and six evaluation sets, with exact and near-duplicate matching and worked examples (Section 4); an estimate of the inflation caused by duplicated samples from four versions of each training set, three seeds, cross-fitting of three further learners and per-epoch curves (Section 5); an exact decomposition of Kendalls 𝜏 into detection and ranking term, with paired tests and human reference that show what each benchmark can resolve (Section 6); protocol built on these results, re-ranking of 33 metrics that includes linear baseline and zero-shot judges, case studies, and released filter lists and code (Section 7). 2. Related work Metrics for image captioning. Two recent surveys organize more than seventy metrics [10, 11]; we follow their grouping into four families. Text-overlap metrics compare candidate with human references by n-grams or scene graphs: BLEU [12], METEOR [13], ROUGE [14], CIDEr [15] and SPICE [16]. Embedding-similarity metrics compare the candidate with the image in the space of contrastive encoder [17]. CLIPScore [18] introduced the idea and needs no references; PAC-S [19] and PACS++ [20] refine the encoder with positive-augmented contrastive learning and remain 4 training-free with respect to human scores. Learned regression metrics fit human scores directly: Polos, DENEB and Pearl. Judges prompt large model for rating: CLAIR [21] and G-VEval [22] call proprietary model, FLEUR [23] uses an open VLM and reads the score from token probabilities, and Rigel fine-tunes such judge on human scores. EXPERT [24] is closest to our topic among the metric papers: its authors noticed that Polaris and Nebula share imagecaption pairs and merged them when building combined training set. They did not examine whether the shared pairs cross the boundary between training and test splits, which is the question we pursue. How metrics are evaluated. Metrics are compared by their correlation with human judgments on Flickr8k [25] and Composite [26], and since 2024, on the test splits of Polaris and Nebula. An earlier re-evaluation asked what these correlations capture [27]. Neighbouring fields have gone further on the statistical side. In machine translation, paired resampling became the standard test [28], and the treatment of ties in Kendalls 𝜏 was shown to change which metric wins [29]. For classifiers, Demšar [30] established that comparisons over several data sets need tests corrected for multiple comparisons. In deep metric learning, Musgrave et al. [8] found that years of reported progress shrank once methods were compared under one protocol. Published tables of captioning metrics still report single correlation per benchmark; we bring these tools to this setting. Duplicates, leakage and contamination. Near-duplicate test images in CIFAR inflate accuracy [31], and rebuilt ImageNet test sets lower it [32]. In open-domain question answering, most test answers also appear in the training data [33]. Leakage is recurring cause of irreproducible results across the sciences that use machine learning [9], and large pretrained models may have seen entire benchmarks [34], images included [35]. Methods to detect such overlap range from hashing to retrieval in feature space [31, 35]; we use both. Networks can memorize individual labels, and the way to measure it is to train with and without an example and compare predictions on it [36]; our cross-fitting design applies this idea to duplicated evaluation samples. Our case differs from these studies in three ways. What is duplicated is not an input but labelled evaluation sample, an image with candidate caption and its human score, and the affected model is itself an evaluator. The duplication happens between sibling collections that are evaluated on each other, not between web-scale corpus and benchmark. And we do not stop at counting overlap but estimate its effect with controlled retraining, matched control and per-epoch doseresponse curve. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first traintest audit of the human-judgment benchmarks on which learned captioning metrics are developed. 3. Benchmarks, terms and statistical tools 3.1. Collections and evaluation sets Polaris [4], Nebula [5] and Spica [6] each provide training, validation and test splits. Every entry consists of an image, human-written reference captions, candidate caption, typically the output of captioning model, and human score on five-level scale. Polos is trained on the Polaris training set, DENEB on that of Nebula, while Pearl and Rigel are trained on that of Spica. We evaluate on the three test sets and on the earlier benchmarks Flickr8k-Expert, Flickr8k-CF [25] and Composite [26]. The collections store judgments in two different ways, and the difference is needed to read every count in this paper  (Table 1)  . Polaris and Spica store one entry per rating: an imagecaption pair that was rated by eight annotators appears eight times, each time with one score. Nebula stores one entry per pair, with the mean of its ratings. The Polaris test set therefore has about three times as many entries as imagecaption pairs. Two further facts follow from the table. First, about two-thirds of the pairs in Polaris (63% in the training set and in the test set) carry single rating, and that rating is almost always the lowest score (99.7%); the pairs that were rated several times make up the rest. Table 3 shows where these pairs fall in the test set. Second, the Spica test set and the Nebula test set are largely one set of judgments in two forms: the Spica test set contains the individual ratings of the Nebula test pairs, and further pairs that mostly carry single lowest score (Appendix C). Results on these two test sets are thus not independent of each other. 6 Table 1: How each set stores human judgments. pair is an image with one candidate caption; sample is one stored entry, which is one rating in Polaris, Spica, and Flickr8k-Expert, and one pair with its mean score elsewhere. Lowest is the share of samples with the lowest score on the scale. Indented lines give the training sets after deduplication (Section 5). Images are counted by pixel content.

We draw whole images, with all their samples, because samples of one image are not independent. Paired comparison. Two metrics evaluated on the same samples share most of their luck: an easy draw of images helps both, and comparing their separate intervals ignores this. We compute the difference between the two metrics on each bootstrap draw and report the interval of that difference [28]. difference whose interval excludes zero is one that the test set can resolve. Correction for multiple comparisons. Among the several hundred pairs that can be formed from more than thirty metrics, some differences look significant by chance 8 alone. Holms procedure [39] raises the bar for each test according to how many tests are made, so that the chance of even one false claim stays below 5%. All statements that two metrics are separated refer to this corrected test. Learned metrics are trained three times with different random seeds, and we report the mean; single training can differ from another by more than the differences between metrics (Section 7). 4. Audit: are there test samples in the training sets? 4.1. Matching by content File names and identifiers are not stable across the collections, so we match content. Two images are the same if their decoded pixels have the same hash; two candidates are the same if their text is identical (details in Appendix D). For training set 𝑇 and an evaluation set, every evaluation sample 𝑠 with image 𝑥𝑠 and candidate 𝑐𝑠 then falls into one of three groups, 𝑔𝑇 (𝑠) = duplicated if (𝑥𝑠, 𝑐𝑠) occurs in 𝑇, image only if 𝑥𝑠 occurs in 𝑇, but not with 𝑐𝑠, (2) unseen image otherwise. 4.2. What is duplicated Samples move between collections. Fig. 2 gives the result for every training set and evaluation set. The Spica training set contains 68.4% of the samples of the Polaris test set, and the Nebula training set contains 50.2%. In the other direction, the Polaris training set contains 43.3% of the Spica test set and 24.4% of the Nebula test set. Within collection, the overlap is small (2.2% for Spica, none for the others). The duplicates carry the same ratings. Fig. 3a shows typical case: the eight ratings of pair appear in the same order in the Polaris test set and in the Spica training set, and the Nebula training set stores their mean. This is the rule. After averaging the ratings of each pair on both sides, the two copies agree exactly for 96.7% of the duplicated pairs between the Spica training set and the Polaris test set, and for 99.9% between the Nebula training set and the Polaris test set (Appendix B). metric trained Figure 2: Share of each evaluation set that is inside each training set. Counting pairs instead of samples. Because the collections store judgments differently, the same overlap looks smaller when counted in pairs: the duplicates in the 10 Spica training set are 32% of the Polaris test pairs. These are the pairs that were rated several times, so they hold 68.4% of the ratings, and it is the ratings over which 𝜏 is computed. Most of the remaining pairs carry single lowest score. Images are shared more widely than judgments. Almost half of the Composite samples show an image that is also in the Spica training set, but only one is duplicated sample. Flickr8k-Expert and Flickr8k-CF share nothing with any training set. 4.3. Exact matching misses little Hashing cannot find photograph that was saved twice (Fig. 3b) or caption that differs by character (Fig. 3c). We therefore repeat the audit with relaxed rule: images match if the cosine similarity of their SigLIP [40] features exceeds 0.97, and candidates match if they are identical after lower-casing and removing punctuation or have character similarity above 0.9. The four large shares rise by less than one percentage point (Appendix B). The exact rule is thus tight lower bound, and all experiments use it. The released filter lists come in both versions; the relaxed one removes slightly more training samples, 45,371 instead of 42,493 from the Spica training set. 5. Doseresponse: the gain grows with every epoch If gain is memorization, more exposure should produce more of it. This is the logic of doseresponse relation: an effect that rises with the dose is hard to attribute to anything else. Here the dose is the number of passes over the training set. The public scripts store checkpoint after every epoch; we scored them all  (Fig. 6)  . 15 Figure 6: Kendalls 𝜏 on the Polaris test set after each training epoch, on duplicated samples (left) and on all other samples (right). Thin lines are single Pearl trainings; thick lines are the mean of the trainings whose training set holds the duplicates (orange) or is deduplicated (blue); numbers are the gap between the two means. Trainings stop at different epochs, so later means average fewer runs. Both panels span the same number of points. DENEB: Appendix F. For Pearl, the trainings whose set holds the duplicates climb by about two points per epoch on the duplicated samples, while the deduplicated trainings stay level; the gap widens from 2.5 to 10.4 points. On all other samples, every checkpoint of every training lies within half point. This comparison follows each model against itself one epoch earlier, so it does not depend on whether the deduplicated set is in some way weaker training set. It also explains why single trainings disagree: the validation score that selects the checkpoint varies by at most 0.5 points between the epochs of run, so the selected epoch, and with it the inflation that one training reports, is close to arbitrary. For DENEB the gap on duplicated samples also opens during the first epochs, but it stays below one point throughout: 0.1 after the first epoch and at most 0.9 later, while all other samples differ by at most 0.15 points (Appendix F). 5.6. Why Pearl gains more than DENEB The label audit rules out one explanation: both training sets hold the test ratings themselves (Section 4), so DENEB is not protected by seeing different labels. Two 16 differences remain, and the evidence supports both. Repetition. The Spica training set stores duplicated pair once per rating, on average 6.4 times, while the Nebula training set stores it once. Pearl thus meets each duplicated pair several times per epoch. The learner. Cross-fitting holds the learner fixed and varies the training set: the same three-layer network gains 8.4 points from the duplicates in the Spica training set and 3.2 from those in the Nebula training set. The per-epoch curves agree: DENEB shows the signature of Pearl at about tenth of the size (0.9 against 10.4 points). The inflation is therefore joint property of how collection stores its judgments and of the model trained on it. split of the duplicates by whether the two copies of the label agree, which would test third explanation, is not possible: fewer than 4% differ. 5.7. Further checks The general cost of deduplication does not explain the gain. model trained on the deduplicated set is slightly weaker everywhere, also where nothing is duplicated: the released model is ahead by +1.11 [+0.93, +1.29] points on Composite, by +1.20 [+0.16, +2.26] on the unseen-image samples of the Polaris test set, and by +0.6 to +1.1 over all samples of the other evaluation sets. This general cost of about one point is the same on Composite and on unseen images, and it is exactly the term that Eq. (3) subtracts. Its likely source is that deduplication deletes every judgment that originates from the Polaris validation and test splits, which the matched control keeps; for the estimate of inflation, the source does not matter, because the gain on duplicated samples differs from the general cost in three ways that loss of useful training data cannot produce. Size. It is +6.45 points against about one, and the difference 𝐼 has an interval far from zero. Place. It appears only on the test samples that the training set contains, and the matched control, which gives up as much data, keeps all of it. Time. The general cost does not grow with training: on Composite, the gap stays between 0.5 and 1.1 points at every epoch (Appendix F). The gap on duplicated samples rises with every pass over the training set, from 2.5 to 10.4 points. model that merely lacks useful data does not fall further behind, pass after pass, on exactly those test samples that its competitor has seen; model that memorizes them does. The gain 𝐼 is therefore consistent with memorization of the duplicated samples; because the comparison is 17 not randomized experiment, it supports this reading rather than proving it. Rigel. Only the inference code and one checkpoint of Rigel are public, so it cannot be retrained. Compared group by group with zero-shot judge that has no training set, its lead is not significantly larger on duplicated samples than on unseen images (Appendix G). The same indirect comparison recovers only about half of the known effect for Pearl, so it cannot exclude an inflation of few points. The exposure is also small: according to its paper, Rigel is fitted to human scores for single epoch, and after one epoch the gap of Pearl is 2.5 points. Published numbers. For the metric that each of the four papers proposes, the training set contains at most 0.1% of any test set reported in that paper; these numbers are not in question. Duplicates enter published tables in two other ways. First, Polos is baseline on the Nebula test set in the DENEB, Pearl and Rigel papers, although its training set contains 24.4% of that set; trained on the released instead of the deduplicated Polaris set, the Polos architecture gains +1.69 [+1.17, +2.22] points there and +2.48 [+2.07, +2.90] on the Spica test set. Second, later metrics are trained on several collections at once. EXPERT [24] is trained on the Polaris and Nebula training sets and reported on both test sets; its released training files contain 13,111 of the 26,122 samples of the Polaris test set (50.2%) and 806 of the 3,298 samples of the Nebula test set (24.4%), matched by image identifier and caption. BEiTScore [42] likewise trains on both training sets and reports both test sets. We have not retrained either and do not claim that their scores are inflated: DENEB shows that duplicates need not inflate metric; Pearl shows that they can. 6. What do the benchmarks measure? 6.1. P1 follows from Section 5: one cannot know in advance which model memorizes, so duplicates are excluded by construction; deduplicated models are used only where needed because deduplication has small cost elsewhere. On the three recent test sets, this CLIP ridge regression is not separated from Polos (differences of 0.6 to +0.2 points); on the earlier benchmarks it is significantly above Polos on Flickr8k-Expert and Flickr8k-CF and below it on Composite. In (a), the candidate is fluent and close to the references in wording but wrong in one fact. Embedding and learned regression metrics place it near the top; the judge, which reads the image and the references together, places it low. This is the typical success of judge. Judges are not uniformly better, however; they are better on average and fail differently, for example, by underrating correct caption on which the other metrics agree with people. Case (b) shows inflation on single sample. Pearl trained on the deduplicated set places the pair far below the human score; Pearl trained on the released set, which holds the pair with its seven ratings, places it much closer. Caption and image are unchanged. 1Strictly, P1 would exclude models trained on the released Spica and Nebula sets from Composite, as each holds one of its 11,982 samples. Because one sample changes 𝜏 by less than 0.04 points and Rigel cannot be retrained, we rank them on Composite. 26 Figure 11: Two pairs from the Polaris test set. Each row shows the image, the candidate (in quotation marks), one of the references, and the mean human score on 01 scale. On the right, bar gives the percentile at which metric places the pair among all pairs of the set that are rated above the lowest score, and the dashed line gives the percentile of the human score. (a) The candidate names two women where the image shows woman and man; learned and embedding metrics rate it high, the judge rates it low, as people do. (b) duplicated sample: Pearl trained without it underrates the pair, and Pearl trained with it (orange) moves most of the way to the human score. Twelve further cases: Appendix J. 7.4. Judges behind proprietary interface We evaluate judges built on open models and do not run CLAIR, G-VEval, or other judges that call proprietary model. There are three reasons, in order of weight. First, protocol must be repeatable: hosted models are updated and withdrawn, so number measured today cannot be reproduced or extended to new evaluation set later. Second, Eq. (9) needs the probabilities of all ten digits, which hosted interfaces expose only in part; Kim et al. [24] report the same limitation for GPT-4o. Third, the training data of proprietary model cannot be audited, which is the very question of this paper. Published results indicate what such judges would add: Kim et al. report for reference-free GPT-4o judge 58.2 on the Polaris test set, 54.3 on the Nebula test set and 65.9 on Composite, close to the range of our open reference-free judges  (Fig. 9)  . These figures come from another implementation and were not measured under our protocol, so we do not rank them; repeatable comparison with proprietary judges remains open. 27 8. Discussion Beyond this family of benchmarks. Nothing in the mechanism is specific to captioning. collection of human judgments is expensive, so new collection reuses the images, systems, and sometimes the judgments of an earlier one; learned evaluator is then tested on both. The same holds for learned metrics in machine translation, summarization and image quality assessment. Three elements of this study transfer directly. Matching by content, not by identifier, finds duplicates that survive renaming. The comparison within test set, by groups and by epoch, separates memorization from the many other consequences of changing training set. And the decomposition of rank correlation into detection and ranking applies to any benchmark whose scale has heavily populated lowest level. More broadly, the reliability of benchmark is an empirical property that can be measured, and measuring it belongs to the evaluation of pattern recognition method as much as the headline number does. Caveats on VLM judges. The pretraining data of the judges is not documented at the level of individual images, so we cannot exclude that they have seen COCO or Flickr images with their reference captions; human scores of candidate captions are far less likely input. All four judges, Rigel included, build on language models of one generation, and judges based on large language models can favour text produced by similar models [46]; the benchmarks studied here cannot test this. judge is also orders of magnitude slower than regression metric. Limitations. The comparison of released and deduplicated training sets is not randomized experiment, and deduplication has general cost of about one point whose source we can only make plausible (Section 5.7); our claims of inflation rest on the within-set, matched and per-epoch comparisons, which subtract it. For Rigel we can report only that no inflation was detected. Whether sharing an image without its candidate has small effect remains open (Section 5.3). We study one family of collections, and three of the six evaluation sets give no human reference. 28 9. Conclusion

sections.title: The three recent collections of human judgments for image captioning made learned
sections.content: metrics possible. Because they were built on one another, samples from their test sets, with the same ratings, are present in the training sets of sibling collections. Whether this inflates metric depends on the learner and on how often training set repeats sample: for Pearl, the gain on duplicated samples grows with every epoch; for DENEB, it is below one point. Independently of duplication, most of the correlation that benchmark tables report measures the detection of captions with the lowest human score, an ability that current metrics share, and the recent test sets do not order the learned regression metrics of their own family; ridge regression on frozen features matches or exceeds all three there. With duplicates excluded by construction and the two abilities reported separately, zero-shot VLM judges rank first on the recent test sets and fine-tuned judge on the earlier benchmarks. We hope that the protocol, the filter lists, and the statistical tools assembled here will be useful for the next generation of learned evaluators, in captioning and beyond.

The released Spica collection Four properties of the public release matter for anyone who trains or tests on it. One image, two identifiers. The 75,535 image identifiers refer to 61,571 distinct images; the others are byte-identical files under second identifier. The splits are disjoint by identifier but not by content: 1,289 of the 3,287 test images (39.2%) are also training images. The test set contains Nebulas. 3,287 of the Nebula test pairs are in the Spica test set with their individual ratings (10,187 samples), and averaging these ratings reproduces the Nebula score in 99.9% of the samples. The Spica test set holds 3,148 further pairs, 89% of which carry single rating with the lowest score. Half of the training samples have no reference. 148,810 of the 333,397 released samples carry an empty reference list, all of them in the training split (48% of it). Own-split duplicates. 342 Spica test samples (2.2%; at most 3.8% with near duplicates) are duplicated in the Spica training split. 33 Appendix D. Implementation details Image and caption matching. An image file is decoded with Pillow and converted to 8-bit RGB; no rotation from EXIF metadata is applied. Its hash is the SHA-1 digest of the string widthxheight followed by the raw RGB bytes. Two files with the same hash therefore show identical pixels, whatever their names, formats or metadata. Candidates are compared as exact strings. The released filter lists contain, for each training set and evaluation set, the hashes of the images and the indices of the duplicated samples; they contain no image, caption or score. Bootstrap and tests. Intervals are percentile intervals over 10,000 draws of images with replacement (1,000 for the group analyses of Section 5 and the cross-fitting). For learned metric the draws of its three seeds are averaged before the interval is taken. The 𝑝-value of paired difference is computed from normal approximation with the bootstrap standard error, because percentile 𝑝-value cannot fall below two over the number of draws, and is then corrected by Holms procedure over all pairs of metrics of an evaluation set. Order accuracy uses 20 random splits of the ratings and draws images in the same way. Ridge regression and network. Both use frozen features in the layout of Polos: from sentence encoder and from visionlanguage encoder, the embeddings of the candidate and of reference, their element-wise product and their absolute difference; and from the visionlanguage encoder also the product and the absolute difference of the candidate and image embeddings. These ten groups are concatenated. The sentence encoder is sup-simcse-roberta-base [43] (a uniform mixture of its 13 layers); the visionlanguage encoder is SigLIP so400m-patch14-384, which gives 9,984 dimensions, or CLIP ViT-B/32 for the rows marked CLIP, which gives 6,144. One feature vector is built per reference; in training each reference is weighted example so that every sample counts once, and at test time the score of sample is the maximum over its references. The ridge penalty is chosen from {0.1, 0.3, 1, 3, 10, 30} by 𝜏 on validation images that are in neither the training set nor any test set. The network has layers of 9,984, 2,304, 1,152 and 1 units with tanh activations and dropout 0.1, and is 34 trained with learning rate of 3 105, batches of 64 with four accumulation steps, and early stopping with patience of five epochs. Polos architecture is the public Polos model trained on cached CLIP features. Folds for cross-fitting are assigned by image. Zero-shot judges. The judges are Qwen/Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct vision ebb281ec), Qwen/Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct (0c351dd0) (reand OpenGVLab/InternVL3_5-8B-HF (741a7d03); Rigel is the released checkpoint (303d2086). All run with transformers 4.57.1 and torch 2.5.1 in bfloat16. An image is passed at the resolution that yields at most 256 visual tokens. In the mode with references, the first five references in the stored order are used. The prompt is the following; the bracketed part is included only in the mode with references. Your task is to evaluate and rate the caption on scale of 0 to 9 based on the given Grading Criteria. (Print the score ONLY) Grading Criteria: 0: The caption does not describe the image at all. 9: The caption accurately and clearly describes the image. [Reference captions written by people for this image: . . . ] Caption: . . . Score (Choose rating from 0 to 9): The score is Eq. (9), computed from the probabilities of the ten digit tokens at the first generated position; each digit is single token in all three tokenizers. For the Qwen3-VL judges these tokens carry nearly all of the probability mass. InternVL3.5 sometimes opens reasoning block first, so we prefill the empty block <think>nn</think>nn and read the rating after it. Reading the score without the prefill, from the renormalized digit probabilities, changes 𝜏 by at most 0. points on five sets but by 2.4 to 3.0 points on Flickr8k-Expert (Table D.1). Details of inference can thus move judge by more than the differences between judges, and they need to be reported. Appendix E. Cases like the first are what the detection term of Eq. (5) rewards. Different wording. Text overlap underrates captions that are right but phrased unlike the references, or that contain misspelt word (Figs. J.1a, J.1c, J.2d). One wrong detail. When fluent caption misnames the animal, the action or the number of people, embedding and learned regression metrics tend to place it high. The judge is closest to people in some of these cases (Figs. J.1b, J.2b, J.2f) and as wrong as the others, or more so, in others (Figs. J.1d, J.2e). Failures of the judge. The judge underrates correct caption with misspelt word (Fig. J.1c) and overrates plausible caption for scene it does not describe (Fig. J.2c), where every other metric agrees with people. Debatable human scores. In Fig. J.1e people rate caption about minor part of the image highly and all metrics place it at the bottom; in Fig. J.1f people give middling score to caption that the judge places at the top. Such cases limit the agreement that any metric can reach and are one reason why the human reference of Eq. (8) is not ceiling.
